# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Glenox Circular Materials, Inc. – Protoux CellTrace Software License: Issues Review
**Privileged & Confidential – Attorney Work Product**

---

## 1. Summary

I reviewed all nine documents in the folder:

1. Software License Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (the "**SLA**")
2. Side Letter on pricing
3. Data Processing Addendum (the "**DPA**")
4. Glenox's notice letter of October 20, 2026
5. Parent Guaranty from Glenox Holdings LLC
6. Statement of Work No. 1
7. Order Form No. 1
8. Kickoff meeting notes
9. Protoux's certificate of insurance

The SLA is governed by New York law (SLA §16.1). It licenses the Platform for one site, Glenox's Rochester, New York hydrometallurgical facility (Order Form §2.1). The commercial terms are:

- an **Annual Subscription Fee of $480,000** (Order Form §3.1), before the 15% Side Letter discount; and
- an **Initial Subscription Term of 60 months (five years)** from March 2, 2026 (Order Form §1.2).

The copies in the file have blank signature blocks. This memo assumes all documents were executed in the form provided, and we should confirm that against the signed versions.

I found five significant issues. In order of urgency:

| # | Issue | Location | Urgency |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unconsented Change of Control from the Sennford sale | SLA §15.2 and §1.3; Notice Letter ¶¶1–3 | **Immediate.** Closing is expected on or about January 15, 2027 |
| 2 | Glenox's DPA indemnity, including regulatory fines, is uncapped | SLA §11.3(b) and §1.8; DPA §9.2 and §10.1 | High |
| 3 | Exclusivity extends to all Glenox Affiliates worldwide, and to Sennford after closing | Side Letter §2; SLA §1.4 | High, and made worse by the sale |
| 4 | Protoux may assign freely, while Glenox cannot | SLA §15.1 | Medium |
| 5 | Auto-renewal for successive five-year terms on a 120-day opt-out | Order Form §4.1 and §1.2 | Medium. The deadline is years away but easy to miss |

The Parent Guaranty makes Issues 1 and 2 worse. It is discussed in Section 3.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1: The Sennford share sale is a Change of Control that needs Protoux's prior written consent, and none has been sought

**Location**
- SLA §1.3, definition of "Change of Control of Licensee"
- SLA §15.2
- SLA §14.3(b) and §14.4
- Glenox Notice Letter dated October 20, 2026, ¶¶1–3

**Why it matters**
- **The sale is a Change of Control.** Under SLA §1.3(a), a Change of Control includes any transfer of more than 50% of Glenox's voting shares, "whether by Licensee or by any holder of its shares." The notice letter reports that on October 14, 2026, Glenox Holdings LLC signed a share purchase agreement to sell **all** of Glenox's shares to **Sennford Resources Corp.** Closing is expected on or about **January 15, 2027**.
- **Glenox has promised not to undergo the change without consent.** Under SLA §15.2, Glenox "shall not undergo a Change of Control of Licensee without Licensor's prior written consent."
- **The notice letter does not obtain that consent.** It is sent "for information purposes only," as a courtesy, and asks for nothing. Glenox's statement that operations will not change does not satisfy §15.2. Protoux's silence will not either, because waivers must be in writing (SLA §17.8).
- **Protoux's remedies are severe.** If closing occurs without consent, Protoux may:
  - terminate on just 10 days' written notice; and
  - declare "all unpaid Subscription Fees for the remainder of the Subscription Term" immediately due, payable within 30 days.
- **The amount at stake is large.** Fees are invoiced annually in advance, so at a January 2027 closing the unpaid fees for Years 2–5 of the Initial Term would be about **$1.92 million** at $480,000 a year. The figure is about $1.63 million if the discounted rate applies.
- **Protoux may argue for more.** "Subscription Term" is defined to include Renewal Terms (SLA §1.18), so Protoux may try to claim fees beyond the Initial Term.
- **Glenox would lose the Platform and still pay.** It would lose access to its Rochester chain-of-custody system and still owe the accelerated fees. These amounts survive termination (SLA §14.3(b), §14.4).
- **The accelerated fees may fall outside the cap.** Arguably they are "Licensee's obligation to pay Fees," which SLA §11.3(d) carves out of the liability cap.
- **Holdings guarantees the whole amount.** Glenox Holdings LLC guarantees it under the Parent Guaranty. That exposure continues after Holdings has sold Glenox (see Section 3).

**Recommended fix**
1. **Before closing**, send Protoux a formal request under SLA §17.1 for its prior written consent to the Change of Control. Alternatively, request a written waiver of §15.2 for the Sennford transaction, signed by an authorized Protoux representative.
2. Have the consent expressly confirm three things:
   - Protoux will not exercise its termination or acceleration rights for this transaction;
   - the Side Letter discount continues; and
   - Sennford and its group will not be treated as "Affiliates" for the exclusivity covenant (see Issue 3).
3. Build Protoux's consent into the share purchase agreement as a closing deliverable or condition. Coordinate with Sennford's deal counsel.
4. In any amendment, narrow §15.2 for the future. Consent should not be unreasonably withheld, and the acceleration remedy should be deleted or capped.

---

### Issue 2: Glenox's DPA indemnity, including regulatory fines, is uncapped

**Location**
- SLA §11.3(b), read with SLA §1.8 (definition of "data protection obligations") and SLA §11.1
- DPA §9.2
- DPA §10.1

**Why it matters**
- **The indemnity is broad.** DPA §9.2 requires Glenox to "indemnify, defend and hold harmless Processor" against "any and all Losses, **including regulatory fines**." It covers:
  - Protoux's processing in line with Glenox's instructions, including Glenox's configuration of the Platform;
  - Glenox's failure to give notices or obtain consents from data subjects; and
  - over-collection of data in breach of DPA §3.3.
- **The data subjects are numerous.** They include drop-off customers, collection and haulage drivers, and employees whose details are recorded in custody and intake records (DPA §3.2, Annex 1).
- **"Losses" is defined widely.** It includes penalties, fines, and notification and remediation costs (DPA §1.4).
- **DPA §10.1 looks like it caps this, but it does not.** It makes DPA liability "subject to the limitations of liability in Section 11 of the Agreement," and Section 11 includes the §11.3 exclusions.
- **SLA §11.3(b) removes the cap.** It provides that the 12-month-fees cap in §11.1, and the exclusion of indirect damages in §11.2, "shall not apply to … either party's data protection obligations." SLA §1.8 defines that term to include all of a party's obligations under the DPA. Glenox's §9.2 indemnity is therefore outside both the cap and the exclusion of consequential loss.
- **The carve-out looks protective of Glenox, but cuts both ways.** It appears aimed at Protoux data breaches. Read with DPA §9.2, it leaves Glenox with **unlimited** exposure, including for regulatory fines and Protoux's indirect losses.
- **The order of precedence does not help.** SLA §2.3 ranks the SLA above the DPA, but the two provisions do not conflict. The SLA carve-out simply applies to the DPA indemnity.
- **The protection is lopsided.** Protoux's own DPA indemnity (DPA §9.1) is a narrower defend-and-pay obligation for third-party claims. It is also uncapped, but Protoux carries $5 million of cyber insurance. We have no indication that Glenox holds equivalent cover.
- **Holdings guarantees this exposure too.** The Parent Guaranty covers "all other obligations" of Glenox under the Contract Documents, "actual or contingent" (Guaranty §1.3).

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend SLA §11.3(b) so that it applies only to **Licensor's** data protection obligations (or to "Licensor's breach of the DPA"). Glenox's liability under DPA §9.2 would then fall back within the §11.1 cap.
2. If Protoux insists on a mutual carve-out, add an express **super-cap** for Glenox's DPA liability, for example one to two times annual fees. Also limit DPA §9.2 to Losses caused by Glenox's breach of law or of DPA §3, and exclude:
   - Losses to the extent caused by Protoux's own breach or negligence; and
   - fines that cannot lawfully be indemnified.
3. In the meantime, Glenox should audit its data-subject notices at drop-off and collection points and its driver and employee privacy notices. This will reduce exposure under DPA §3.2. The Design Document's personal-data field mapping, flagged in the kickoff notes, is a useful starting point.

---

### Issue 3: The Side Letter exclusivity extends to all Glenox Affiliate operations worldwide, not just the Rochester site

**Location**
- Side Letter §2.1 and §2.2, and §1.1 (which adopts SLA definitions)
- SLA §1.4, definition of "Covered Operations"
- Order Form §2.1 (Licensed Site)
- Side Letter §4.2 (remedies)

**Why it matters**
- **The covenant borrows a very broad definition.** In return for a 15% discount, Glenox must use the Platform "as its exclusive traceability and process analytics software for Covered Operations." It also must not license, develop or use any Competing Software for Covered Operations during the Subscription Term, including Renewal Terms (Side Letter §5.3). "Covered Operations" takes its meaning from SLA §1.4: "all battery collection, sorting, processing and materials recovery activities of Licensee and **its Affiliates, wherever located**."
- **The definition was written for a different purpose.** Within the SLA it only sets the scope of support and warranty coverage (SLA §6.1, §10.2), where its breadth helps Glenox. Imported into the Side Letter, it turns a single-site licence into a **group-wide, worldwide** exclusivity covenant.
- **The covenant goes well beyond the licence.** It would cover lead-acid and other battery lines and every other facility of Glenox and its Affiliates. Yet the licence itself covers only the Rochester lithium-ion hydrometallurgical facility (Order Form §2.1; SLA §4.1), and new sites need a new Order Form (SLA §4.3).
- **The sale makes it worse.** An "Affiliate" is any entity that controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with Glenox (SLA §1.1). After closing, **Sennford Resources Corp.** and its whole group become Glenox Affiliates. Their existing traceability or process analytics systems could put Glenox in breach.
- **The order of precedence does not help.** The Side Letter does not conflict with the SLA or the Order Form. It borrows the SLA's definition.
- **Breach has financial consequences.** If a breach is not cured within 30 days, Protoux may:
  - withdraw the discount for the rest of the Subscription Term; and
  - claw back the discount from the date of breach, about **$72,000 a year**.

  Those remedies are "in addition to any other rights" (Side Letter §4.3), which leaves room for a material-breach argument under SLA §14.1.
- **The covenant may block integration.** It could constrain Sennford's post-closing integration plans and is likely to come up in buyer diligence.

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend Side Letter §2 to replace "Covered Operations" with a new defined term limited to **lithium-ion battery chain-of-custody, feedstock intake and process analytics activities conducted at the Licensed Site**.
2. Expressly exclude:
   - other facilities and Affiliates; and
   - any person that becomes an Affiliate through an acquisition of or by Glenox, including Sennford and its subsidiaries.
3. Add a sunset or termination right for the exclusivity on a Change of Control, so that Glenox can choose between keeping the discount and keeping the exclusivity.
4. Raise this in the same correspondence as the Change of Control consent (Issue 1), because the Sennford transaction is what brings it to a head.

---

### Issue 4: Protoux may assign the SLA to anyone without Glenox's consent, while Glenox cannot assign

**Location**
- SLA §15.1
- Also relevant: Parent Guaranty §9.1, under which the Guaranty benefits Protoux's "successors and assigns"

**Why it matters**
- **The clause is one-sided.** Glenox may not assign, including by operation of law, without Protoux's prior written consent. By contrast, Protoux "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Licensee's consent to any person, including by merger, consolidation, reorganization or sale of all or any part of its assets or business."
- **Nothing limits Protoux's choice of assignee.** There is no restriction on who the assignee is, no notice requirement, and no Glenox termination right.
- **Glenox's most sensitive data could go to a rival.** Protoux could transfer the contract, and with it hosted access to Glenox's Customer Data, to a **competing battery recycler**. That data includes chain-of-custody records, supplier and offtaker information, recovery yields and process parameters (SLA §1.5, §13.1).
- **Glenox could end up with a weaker vendor.** Protoux could also assign to a financially weaker vendor, or split the contract "in part," so that support and hosting come from different entities.
- **Glenox could not easily walk away.** Glenox would remain locked into five years of fees, plus exclusivity and auto-renewal, with no exit.

**Recommended fix**
1. Make §15.1 mutual. Neither party should assign without the other's consent, not to be unreasonably withheld.
2. At a minimum, permit Protoux to assign only:
   - the **whole** Agreement;
   - to a successor to all or substantially all of its business;
   - that is **not a Glenox competitor** (for example, not engaged in battery collection, recycling or materials recovery); and
   - that assumes all obligations in writing.
3. Require prior written notice to Glenox of any assignment.
4. Give Glenox a right to terminate without penalty, with a pro-rata refund of prepaid fees and data export under SLA §8.6, if the assignee is a competitor or does not meet reasonable financial or security standards.
5. Add a reciprocal right for Glenox to assign to an Affiliate or acquirer without consent.

---

### Issue 5: The Order Form auto-renews for successive five-year terms unless Glenox opts out at least 120 days before expiry

**Location**
- Order Form §4.1, read with Order Form §1.2 and §3.4
- SLA §3.1 and §2.3 (the Order Form ranks first in the order of precedence)

**Why it matters**
- **Each renewal runs another five years.** The subscription "renews automatically for successive Renewal Terms equal in length to the Initial Subscription Term." The Initial Term is 60 months, so each renewal binds Glenox for another **five years**, about **$2.4 million** per Renewal Term at $480,000 a year.
- **Fees cannot go down on renewal.** Renewal fees carry forward at the fee in effect at the end of the preceding term (Order Form §3.4).
- **The opt-out window is narrow and easy to miss.** Glenox can avoid renewal only by giving written non-renewal notice **at least 120 days before** the end of the then-current term, in the form SLA §17.1 requires. That chance comes once every five years.
- **The first deadline is in 2030.** The Initial Term ends on or about March 1–2, 2031, so the first non-renewal deadline falls around **early November 2030**.
- **Protoux need not remind Glenox.** Nothing obliges Protoux to warn Glenox before the window closes.
- **Other provisions run for the renewal period too.** A missed deadline also extends the Side Letter exclusivity, which lasts for "any Renewal Term" (Side Letter §5.3), and potentially enlarges any Change of Control acceleration claim (Issue 1).

**Recommended fix**
1. Amend Order Form §4.1 so that Renewal Terms are **12 months**, with non-renewal notice of no more than 60–90 days.
2. In the alternative, or in addition:
   - require Protoux to give written notice of the upcoming renewal deadline at least 60 days before the window opens; and
   - give Glenox a right to terminate for convenience during any Renewal Term on 90 days' notice, without acceleration.
3. Cap renewal-term fee increases.
4. In the meantime, docket the deadline in Glenox's and our contract management systems now.

---

## 3. Related observation: the Parent Guaranty amplifies Issues 1 and 2

**Location:** Parent Guaranty §1.3, §2.1, §3.2(a), §6.1 and §9.1

- **The Guaranty is very wide.** Glenox Holdings LLC guarantees payment **and performance** of all of Glenox's obligations under all Contract Documents, "actual or contingent." That includes:
  - the uncapped DPA indemnity (Issue 2); and
  - any Change of Control acceleration (Issue 1).
- **Amendments and renewals carry through.** The Guaranty is not released by renewals or amendments (Guaranty §3.2(a)). It runs until the SLA ends and all obligations are paid (Guaranty §6.1), so auto-renewals (Issue 5) extend it as well.
- **Holdings stays liable after selling Glenox.** After the Sennford sale, Holdings would remain guarantor for a company it no longer owns or controls.
- **Recommended fix:**
  - As part of the consent request, ask Protoux to **release Holdings** at closing, in exchange for a replacement guaranty from Sennford if Protoux requires one.
  - Coordinate with deal counsel so the share purchase agreement allocates this risk. For example, Sennford could indemnify Holdings for post-closing guaranty claims.
  - In any event, the Issue 2 fix should cap the guaranteed exposure.

## 4. Documents reviewed with no material issues

- **Statement of Work No. 1.** It is consistent with the single-site scope.
- **Kickoff meeting notes.** These confirm the Rochester-only scope and say they do not amend the contract documents. They raise no issue.
- **Protoux's certificate of insurance.** It evidences $5 million each of technology E&O and cyber cover, consistent with SLA §17.5. All of the policies expire on **January 1, 2027**, so Glenox should request an updated certificate after renewal.

## 5. Recommended next steps

1. **This week:** send Protoux a formal consent and waiver request under SLA §15.2. Include the related asks:
   - the Side Letter carve-out for Sennford Affiliates;
   - release of the Holdings guaranty; and
   - continuation of the discount.

   Brief Sennford's counsel and make Protoux's consent a closing deliverable.
2. Package Issues 2–5 as a proposed SLA, DPA, Side Letter and Order Form amendment. The consent request gives us negotiating leverage; Protoux will want to keep a $480,000-a-year customer through the transaction.
3. Docket the November 2030 non-renewal deadline. Request Protoux's renewed certificate of insurance after January 1, 2027.

Please let me know if you would like me to draft the consent request or the amendment.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** Associate
**Date:** November 20, 2026
**Re:** Glenox Circular Materials, Inc. – Protoux CellTrace Software License: Issues Review

---

## 1. Summary

You asked me to review the nine documents in the Glenox / Protoux folder and to identify the issues affecting Glenox's position. The folder contains:

- the Software License Agreement dated March 2, 2026 (New York law);
- the pricing side letter;
- the Data Processing Addendum;
- Glenox's October 20, 2026 notice letter;
- the Glenox Holdings LLC parent guaranty;
- Statement of Work No. 1;
- Order Form No. 1;
- the kickoff meeting notes; and
- Protoux's certificate of insurance.

**Key commercial terms**

- **Licensed Site:** the Rochester, New York lithium-ion hydrometallurgical facility (Order Form §2.1).
- **Annual Subscription Fee:** $480,000 per year (Order Form §3.1).
- **Initial Subscription Term:** 60 months (five years) from March 2, 2026 (Order Form §1.2). It therefore runs to March 2, 2031.
- **Undiscounted value:** about $2.4 million over the initial term.

**Priority issues**

I have identified four issues. The most urgent is the pending sale of Glenox to Sennford Resources Corp. Closing is expected on or about **January 15, 2027**. The sale is a Change of Control that requires Protoux's prior written consent, and Glenox has not asked for it. The other three issues are:

- Protoux's unrestricted right to assign;
- a side letter exclusivity covenant that, read with the License Agreement's definitions, extends worldwide across all Glenox affiliates; and
- a five-year auto-renewal with a 120-day opt-out window.

---

## 2. Issues

### Issue 1 – Pending Sennford sale is an unconsented Change of Control

**Location**
- License Agreement (D1), §1.3 (definition of "Change of Control of Licensee") and §15.2.
- Glenox notice letter dated October 20, 2026 (D4), paragraphs 1–3.
- Related: Parent Guaranty (D5), §§1.3 and 2.1.

**What the documents say**

Section 1.3(a) defines a Change of Control of Licensee to include any transfer of more than 50% of Licensee's voting shares, "whether by Licensee or by any holder of its shares."

Section 15.2 provides that Licensee "shall not undergo a Change of Control of Licensee without Licensor's prior written consent." If that happens, Protoux may:
- terminate on 10 days' written notice; and
- declare "all unpaid Subscription Fees for the remainder of the Subscription Term immediately due and payable," payable within 30 days.

The notice letter reports two things:
- On October 14, 2026, Glenox Holdings LLC signed a share purchase agreement to sell **all** outstanding shares of Glenox to Sennford Resources Corp.
- Closing is expected on or about January 15, 2027.

The letter states that it is sent "for information purposes only, as a courtesy." It does not request consent.

**Why it matters for Glenox**

1. **The sale falls squarely within §1.3(a).** It is a 100% share transfer by Glenox's shareholder. The letter's assurance that Glenox's name, management and operations will not change is irrelevant to the definition.
2. **The letter is not consent.** Section 17.8 requires any waiver to be in writing, and silence or non-objection from Protoux does not count. On closing, therefore, Glenox will be in breach of §15.2.
3. **The financial exposure is severe.** If Protoux terminates after closing in mid-January 2027, roughly four years and two months of the Initial Subscription Term will remain. At $480,000 a year, that is about **$1.9–2.0 million**, depending on how the annual-in-advance billing has been applied. All of it could become payable within 30 days.
4. **Glenox would pay and lose the service.** Termination also ends Glenox's licence (§14.3(a)). The Rochester chain-of-custody system would go dark after only 60 days of data export (§8.6).
5. **The exposure reaches the parent and the deal.** The accelerated sum is a Guaranteed Obligation under the Parent Guaranty (§§1.3, 2.1). Glenox Holdings LLC, the seller, would therefore be exposed as well. The point will also likely need to be disclosed or covered in the share purchase agreement.
6. **Protoux gains negotiating leverage.** Protoux may use the consent requirement to reopen pricing or other terms.

**Recommended fix**

- Before closing, Glenox should send Protoux a formal written request for consent to the Sennford transaction under §15.2.
- Glenox should obtain a signed consent and waiver, executed as required by §17.8. The waiver should cover both the termination right and the acceleration right in relation to this transaction.
- The request should be sent promptly, given the January 15, 2027 target. Coordinate with Glenox's M&A counsel so that Protoux consent is listed as a closing condition or deliverable in the share purchase agreement.
- If an amendment is being negotiated anyway (see the other issues), Glenox should also seek to:
  - delete the acceleration remedy;
  - replace the consent requirement with a notice-only obligation; or
  - at minimum, add a "consent not to be unreasonably withheld, conditioned or delayed" standard and a carve-out for transfers to acquirers that are not Protoux competitors.

---

### Issue 2 – Protoux may assign freely; Glenox may not

**Location**
- License Agreement (D1), §15.1.
- Related: Parent Guaranty (D5), §9.1.

**What the documents say**

Glenox may not assign "whether by operation of law or otherwise" without Protoux's prior written consent. By contrast, Protoux "may assign this Agreement, in whole or in part, without Licensee's consent to any person, including by merger, consolidation, reorganization or sale of all or any part of its assets or business."

There is no requirement of notice to Glenox and no restriction on who the assignee may be. Glenox has no termination right if Protoux assigns.

Under §9.1 of the Parent Guaranty, the guaranty benefits Protoux's "successors and assigns." Any assignee would therefore also take the benefit of Glenox Holdings' guaranty.

**Why it matters for Glenox**

1. **Glenox's data could pass to a competitor.** The Platform holds Glenox's most commercially sensitive information, including chain-of-custody records, feedstock supplier and offtaker data, recovery yields for lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese, and process parameters. Protoux could transfer the contract, and with it the hosting of that Customer Data, to a competing battery recycler or a competitor's affiliate.
2. **Glenox could end up with a weaker counterparty.** The contract could pass to a financially weaker or less capable vendor. Glenox would remain locked into $480,000 a year for the full term with no exit.
3. **Partial assignment creates operational risk.** "In whole or in part" lets Protoux split obligations, such as support versus hosting, among different entities. That would complicate accountability for service levels and data handling.
4. **The asymmetry is stark.** Glenox, by contrast, cannot even undergo a share sale without consent (Issue 1).

**Recommended fix**

Amend §15.1 so that either:
- assignment is mutual, with either party able to assign without consent only to a successor to all or substantially all of its business or assets; or
- at minimum, Protoux's right to assign is conditioned on all of the following:
  - the assignee acquires all or substantially all of Protoux's business relating to the Platform;
  - the assignee is not a competitor of Glenox (for example, not engaged in battery recycling or materials recovery);
  - the assignee assumes all obligations in writing;
  - Glenox receives prior written notice (for example, 30 days); and
  - Glenox has a right to terminate without penalty, with a pro-rata refund of prepaid Fees and full data export, if the assignee is objectionable on reasonable grounds.

Partial assignments should require Glenox's consent.

---

### Issue 3 – Side letter exclusivity reaches all Glenox and affiliate operations worldwide

**Location**
- Side Letter (D2), §§1.1, 2.1, 2.2 and 4.2.
- License Agreement (D1), §1.4 (definition of "Covered Operations") and §1.1 (definition of "Affiliate").
- Order Form (D7), §2.1 (Licensed Site).

**What the documents say**

In exchange for a 15% discount on Subscription Fees (Side Letter §3.1), Glenox agrees to two things:
- to use the Platform "as its exclusive traceability and process analytics software for Covered Operations" (§2.1); and
- not to "license, procure, develop or use any Competing Software for Covered Operations" during the Subscription Term (§2.2).

The side letter does not define Covered Operations itself. It borrows the License Agreement definition (§1.1), which is "all battery collection, sorting, processing and materials recovery activities of Licensee **and its Affiliates, wherever located**" (D1 §1.4).

"Affiliate" includes any entity controlling, controlled by or under common control with Glenox (D1 §1.1).

The licence itself, however, covers only the Rochester, New York hydrometallurgical facility (Order Form §2.1; D1 §4.1). Adding any other site requires a new Order Form (D1 §4.3).

**Why it matters for Glenox**

1. **The covenant is far broader than the licence.** Within the License Agreement, the wide "Covered Operations" definition helps Glenox, because it widens Protoux's support and warranty obligations (D1 §§6.1, 10.2). Imported into the side letter, the same definition does the opposite. It bars Glenox, its parent and every sister company from using any competing traceability or process analytics tool at any facility anywhere in the world. That includes:
   - lead-acid lines;
   - collection and sorting operations;
   - other recovery plants; and
   - future sites.
   Yet only one site is licensed. Glenox cannot comply at other sites without buying more Protoux licences.
2. **The Sennford sale makes it worse.** After closing, Sennford Resources Corp. and its group will become Glenox Affiliates under §1.1, because they will control Glenox. Read literally, the exclusivity would then extend to Sennford's own global operations. That could:
   - put Glenox in breach immediately on closing if Sennford uses competing software; or
   - constrain Sennford's systems choices.

   This is a significant point to flag to the buyer, and it may affect deal terms.
3. **Breach carries a retroactive clawback.** On an uncured breach, Protoux may withdraw the discount for the rest of the Subscription Term, **effective from the date of breach**, and invoice the discount already applied (§4.2). Its other remedies are preserved (§4.3). The discount is worth $72,000 a year (15% of $480,000).
4. **Glenox must certify compliance.** An officer must give annual compliance certifications on request (§4.1). That creates a personal-certification risk given how wide the covenant is.
5. **Precedence does not help.** The side letter does not conflict with the License Agreement or the Order Form. It simply adopts the Agreement's definition. Section 5.1 of the side letter confirms that it supplements the Agreement.
6. **The covenant may outlast the initial term.** It runs for the full Subscription Term, including renewals (§5.3), and therefore interacts with Issue 4.

**Recommended fix**

Amend the side letter so that the exclusivity applies only to:
- the Licensed Site (Rochester); and
- the lithium-ion chain-of-custody, feedstock intake, process analytics and recovery reporting functions actually licensed under the Order Form.

For example, replace "Covered Operations" in §§2.1–2.2 with a new defined term such as "Licensed Operations."

The amendment should also:
- expressly exclude Glenox Holdings LLC, sister companies, and any future acquirer (including Sennford Resources Corp.) and that acquirer's affiliates;
- confirm that later-added sites are covered only if the parties so agree in writing;
- limit the remedy for breach to prospective withdrawal of the discount, with no retroactive clawback; and
- limit the exclusivity to the Initial Subscription Term.

This should be done together with the Change of Control consent in Issue 1.

---

### Issue 4 – Automatic five-year renewals on a 120-day opt-out window

**Location**
- Order Form (D7), §4.1, read with §§1.2, 1.3 and 3.4.
- License Agreement (D1), §§1.18, 2.3 and 3.1.

**What the documents say**

The Initial Subscription Term is 60 months (Order Form §1.2). At its end, the subscription "renews automatically for successive Renewal Terms equal in length to the Initial Subscription Term" unless either party gives non-renewal notice "at least 120 days before the end of the then-current term" (§4.1).

The Annual Subscription Fee for each Renewal Term carries over at the rate in effect at the end of the preceding term (§3.4).

Section 3.1 of the License Agreement defers to the Order Form on term, and the Order Form ranks first in the order of precedence (D1 §2.3).

**Why it matters for Glenox**

1. **Each missed window locks in another five years.** Every renewal commits Glenox to another 60 months at $480,000 a year, which is **about $2.4 million per Renewal Term**, before the side letter discount.
2. **The opt-out window comes once every five years.** For the initial term ending March 2, 2031, notice must be received (§17.1, effective on receipt) by about **November 2, 2030**. Nothing obliges Protoux to send a reminder.
3. **Other terms are locked in too.** The renewal also extends:
   - the side letter exclusivity (Issue 3);
   - the Parent Guaranty; and
   - Protoux's acceleration remedy under §15.2, which reaches all unpaid fees "for the remainder of the Subscription Term," including any Renewal Term.
4. **There is no exit for convenience.** Glenox has no termination-for-convenience right. During a renewal it would be committed for the full five years even if its technology needs change, for example after integration into the Sennford group.

**Recommended fix**

Amend Order Form §4.1 so that renewals are for successive 12-month terms, not 60-month terms. In addition, Glenox should seek one or more of:
- a reduced non-renewal notice period (for example, 60 days);
- an obligation on Protoux to send written renewal reminders at least 60 days before the notice deadline, with no auto-renewal if it fails to do so;
- a Glenox right to terminate for convenience during any Renewal Term on, say, 90 days' notice, with a pro-rata refund; and
- a cap on fee increases at renewal.

In the meantime, Glenox should diarise the November 2030 deadline.
